stem: This is a Windows workstation. What is its default gateway?
explain: ipconfig lists the Ethernet adapter's settings; the Default Gateway line is 192.168.10.1 (gw-01), the router every packet for another network is sent to. ipconfig is the Windows counterpart of ip addr and ip route. Recording the gateway, address and DNS servers belongs to a workstation's configuration baseline; a wrong gateway or DNS server is a common sign of tampering or a rogue DHCP server.

stem: Asset inventories and switch port security identify a network card by its physical (MAC) address. What is this workstation's physical address? (Windows writes it with dashes; either form is accepted.)
explain: ipconfig /all adds the details plain ipconfig leaves out: Physical Address 52-54-00-5E-1C-88, the DHCP server, the lease times and the DNS servers. A MAC address is easy to change, so it is a convenient identifier for inventories and port security but not proof of identity.

stem: Which line shows the router this PC uses to reach other networks?

options.text: Default Gateway: 192.168.10.1
IPv4 Address: 192.168.10.50
options.why: That is this PC's own address.

options.text: Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0
options.why: The mask says which addresses are local, not where the router is.

options.text: Connection-specific DNS Suffix: office.lan
options.why: That is the domain suffix added to short names.

explain: The default gateway is where packets for other networks are sent. A wrong gateway is a common sign of misconfiguration or a rogue DHCP server.

stem: What does the subnet mask 255.255.255.0 tell you?

options.text: The PC can only talk to 255 hosts in total, no matter where they are
options.why: The mask limits the local network, not the total number of hosts you can reach.

options.text: The first three numbers name the network, so 192.168.10.x is local
The router's address is 255.255.255.0, shown on the gateway line
options.why: The router is the default gateway line.

options.text: The PC is on a network of 255 separate subnets, one per host number
options.why: The mask describes one network (a /24).

explain: 255.255.255.0 is the same as /24: addresses that match in the first three octets are on the local network and reached directly.

stem: Which lines show that this PC got its address automatically?

options.text: Node Type: Hybrid, the NetBIOS name resolution setting
options.why: Node type is how NetBIOS names are resolved.

options.text: Host Name: ws-win, the name the computer calls itself
options.why: The host name is the computer's name.

options.text: DHCP Enabled: Yes, with the DHCP Server 192.168.10.1
Physical Address: 52-54-00-5E-1C-88, the address of the network card
options.why: The physical address is fixed in the network card.

explain: DHCP Enabled and the lease lines show the address was leased from a DHCP server. The readme on this PC says gateway and DNS come from DHCP too.

stem: Which line shows the server this PC asks to resolve names?

options.text: DHCP Server: 192.168.10.1
options.why: That hands out addresses, it does not answer DNS questions.

options.text: Default Gateway: 192.168.10.1
options.why: That is the router.

options.text: Primary Dns Suffix: (blank)
options.why: A suffix is a domain name, not a server.

options.text: DNS Servers: 192.168.10.5

explain: DNS Servers lists the resolvers in use: 192.168.10.5. nslookup asks the same server unless you name another.

stem: What is this PC's physical (MAC) address?

options.why: That is the IPv4 address.
That is the DHCPv6 DUID, a client identifier, not the MAC.

options.text: fe80::87e6:e3e8:faaf:621b
options.why: That is the link-local IPv6 address.

explain: Windows writes MAC addresses with dashes on the Physical Address line. The DUID looks similar but is a different identifier.

stem: Why do switch port security and asset inventories use MAC addresses?

options.text: A MAC address never changes and cannot be faked, so it proves which device it is
options.why: MAC addresses can be spoofed, so they are a weak control on their own.

options.text: A MAC address names the network card, so a switch can allow only known devices
A MAC address shows who the user is, so the switch can allow only that person
options.why: It identifies a card, not a person.

options.text: A MAC address is routed across the internet, so it can be checked from anywhere
options.why: MACs only matter on the local network segment.

explain: MAC addresses make a convenient device identifier, but spoofing is easy, so they support a defence rather than replace authentication.

stem: Which command shows the physical address on a Windows PC?

options.text: ipconfig
options.why: Plain ipconfig leaves out the physical address.

options.text: ipconfig /release
options.why: That gives up the DHCP lease.

options.text: ipconfig /all
ipconfig /flushdns
options.why: That clears the local DNS cache.

explain: ipconfig on its own prints a short summary; /all adds the host name, physical address, DHCP and DNS details.

stem: How far does the MAC address of this PC travel?

options.text: All the way to the web server on the internet, unchanged
options.why: Each router rewrites the link-layer addresses.

options.text: Only inside the PC, between the network card and the system
options.why: It is used on the wire to reach the switch and the gateway.

options.text: To the DNS server only, and not to anything else on the network
options.why: It is used for all local delivery, not just DNS.

options.text: Only across the local segment; each router replaces it

explain: Layer 2 addresses are for the next hop on the local link; IP addresses are the end-to-end ones.
